Average Pass@1 (left) and Pass@4 (right) over nine multimodal benchmarks across Qwen3-VL-Thinking sizes. At 8B, AXPO surpasses the 32B Base baseline on Pass@4 while outperforming GRPO at every scale. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) with extended reasoning capabilities have made remarkable progress, producing chains of thought that rival much larger models on mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . These reasoning models invest test-time compute into internal search and reflection to arrive at accurate answers. However, many real-world problems lie beyond what internal reasoning alone can resolve: retrieving up-to-date knowledge, performing complex numerical computation, and understanding fine-grained visual details all require access to external resources [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Tools such as web search, code interpreters, and image manipulation utilities can fill this gap, enabling what we call Multimodal Agentic Reasoning : the model autonomously decides when to think further and when to act through tools, much as it learns to allocate thinking budget, but now extended to interaction with environments [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Figure 2 : Concept. AXPO concentrates exploration on the tool call for agentic reasoning. Left: under GRPO, tool-using rollouts are scarce and often fail, leaving no positive learning signal at the tool call where it is most needed. Right: AXPO fixes the thinking prefix from the failed rollout and resamples the tool call and its continuation, recovering a correct rollout and producing a positive learning signal on the tool call. Agentic reasoning carries a deeper asymmetry between its two constituent behaviors: Thinking and Tool use (Acting) . Thinking is the default mode, self-contained within the model’s token space: every token is under its control and errors can be corrected by exploring a different chain of thought [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Tool use , by contrast, is an auxiliary behavior that is simultaneously powerful but fragile: a short token sequence triggers an external response the model cannot predict or control, and small changes in the call can produce drastically different outcomes (e.g., invalid python code with wrong indent) [ 18 ] . Reasoning models are heavily post-trained for thinking, but far less for acting. We refer to this asymmetry between a safe default and a high-variance auxiliary as the Thinking-Acting Gap . Due to this gap, eliciting agentic reasoning remains a challenge despite the capabilities of recent reasoning VLMs [ 19 ] . Relying solely on prompting is often insufficient to ensure an appropriate tool call when needed. This necessitates post-training pipelines, such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), as evidenced in Figure 1 . SFT reliably teaches the mechanics of tool use but struggles to teach the model to utilize tools better for situations the teacher’s demonstrations did not cover. The resulting agent inherits the teacher’s failure modes and often plateaus near its performance [ 20 , 21 ] . Therefore, the model requires a training signal that goes beyond imitation, which motivates utilizing RL with verifiable outcome rewards after SFT [ 18 , 22 , 23 ] . However, RL methods such as GRPO [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] are suboptimal to make models proficient at acting, because two patterns suppress the tool-call learning signal. First, tool use remains a minority of rollouts compared with thinking-only ( 3(a) ). Second, when tool use is attempted, the entire group of rollouts is far more likely to fail together ( 3(b) ). Under GRPO, this asymmetry weakens the tool-call learning signal in both regimes: tool-using rollouts trail thinking-only successes in mixed groups (negative advantage) and zero out in all-wrong groups [ 27 , 28 ] . These observations motivate targeted exploration for tool use during RL. This raises a critical question: how can we effectively induce such exploration? The Thinking-Acting Gap suggests the answer. Thinking is the native mode of the model and the tool call is the separate mode that turns an intent into a concrete action where the same intent admits diverse implementations ( 3(c) ). Building on this observation, our key insight is that resampling at the tool call lets the model explore diverse agentic reasoning: we anchor the thinking prefix and resample the tool call and its continuation ( Figure 2 ). We call this tool-call resampling . The operation has no analog in pure reasoning, where there is no comparable boundary between a committed intent and a high-variance action. When a tool-using trajectory fails, the thinking prefix may be entirely sound. Re-deriving the full trajectory from scratch wastes budget on prefixes that were not the bottleneck, whereas tool-call resampling concentrates exploration precisely where the Thinking-Acting Gap manifests. We propose AXPO ( A gent e X plorative P olicy O ptimization) based on this principle to narrow the gap during RL. Concretely, AXPO instantiates three design choices on top of a small extra rollout budget: (1) where to resample , only on all-wrong tool-using subgroups where a single recovery flips the GRPO advantage; (2) which prefix , the highest-uncertainty ones; and (3) how resamples enter the gradient , a per-prefix GRPO advantage on continuations and a binary recovery indicator on the source prefix. Unlike prior reward-shaping methods [ 18 , 23 , 29 ] or rollout scaling methods [ 30 , 31 ] , AXPO restructures the rollout distribution itself at the locus of the Thinking-Acting Gap. Across nine multimodal benchmarks at Qwen3-VL-Thinking 2B/4B/8B [ 19 ] , SFT + AXPO outperforms SFT + GRPO at average with Pass@4 gains of + 2.8 +2.8 / + 2.3 +2.3 / + 1.8 +1.8 pp. At 8B, SFT + AXPO surpasses the 32B Base on Pass@4 and reaches 99 % 99\% of its Pass@1, despite using 4 × 4\times fewer parameters ( Figure 1 ). The improvement concentrates on tool-intensive benchmarks, while preserving the performance improvement in reasoning benchmarks compared to SFT + GRPO baseline. Notably, + 25 % +25\% extra resampling budget with AXPO delivers + 1.1 +1.1 pp over + 100 % +100\% extra rollout budget with GRPO, confirming that the gain comes from where compute is spent. Our contributions are as follows: • We identify the Thinking-Acting Gap , an asymmetry between thinking and tool use that manifests in group-based agentic RL as two symptoms: tool use is attempted on 30% of rollouts and tool-using subgroups (the tool-using rollouts within a group) are all-wrong on 40% of questions, yielding non-positive advantage on tool-call tokens. • We propose AXPO , an RL algorithm that closes the gap via tool-call resampling : for all-wrong tool-using subgroups, AXPO fixes the thinking prefix at uncertain tool calls and resamples from them, provably dominating from-scratch sampling on tool-use coverage at fixed budget. • We validate AXPO on nine multimodal benchmarks across three scales of Qwen3-VL-Thinking, with gains for all sizes compared to GRPO baseline, and the resulting 2B model matches the 8B Base and the 8B model surpasses the 32B Base on Pass@4 . 2 Analysis of RL in Agentic Reasoning 2.1 Preliminaries Agentic Reasoning. We study the agentic reasoning of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) π θ \pi_{\theta} given an input 𝒙 {\bm{x}} (text question with visual image) and instruction prompt ( A.2 ), interleaving thinking and tool use. Our tool set covers three standard [ 7 , 18 , 23 ] : a Python interpreter, a web search, and an image zoom-in tool. RL training with GRPO. Our starting point is the standard agentic post-training pipeline [ 18 , 23 ] : supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories followed by reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. Given an input 𝒙 {\bm{x}} , the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} generates a group of N N rollouts { τ i } i = 1 N \{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , each receiving a binary outcome reward r i ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{i}\in\{0,1\} based on answer correctness. We defer the explicit form of ℒ clip \mathcal{L}_{\text{clip}} in Appendix A.1 . 2.2 Diagnosing the Thinking-Acting Gap (a) Proportion of questions by tool-using rollout count (8 rollouts/question) across RL steps under GRPO. (b) All-wrong rate by subgroup type under GRPO: the tool-using fails together far more than the no-tool. (c) Semantic cluster count of 16 resampled tool calls from a fixed failed-rollout prefix, per tool type. Figure 3 : Empirical analysis of diagnosing the Thinking-Acting Gap ( Section 2.2 ). (a) Tool use is under-attempted. (b) The tool-using subgroup (the tool-using rollouts within a GRPO group) fails all-together far more often than the no-tool subgroup. (c) Resampling at a fixed prefix preserves substantive diversity in the tool call, confirming it as a real divergence point. We now ground the Thinking-Acting Gap in three diagnostic measurements collected during RL training ( Figure 3 ). Our starting point is the SFT checkpoint, trained with GRPO [ 24 ] on outcome rewards. Tool use is under-attempted. A defining property of agentic reasoning, unlike conventional agentic RL [ 31 , 33 ] , is that tool use is optional : the model can either produce a <tool_call> tag or skip straight to <answer> . This optionality makes action fragile under RL. We track the fraction of rollouts that contain at least one tool call over the course of RL. As shown in 3(a) , which bins each question by its tool-using rollout count among N = 8 N=8 , the corresponding rollout-level tool-use rate is roughly 27% at step 1 and stays in the 20–35% range over RL training, well below the thinking-only majority. GRPO exerts no pressure to grow the tool-using minority, and the behavior that distinguishes agentic from non-agentic reasoning remains under-represented in each group. When attempted, the tool-using subgroup is prone to being all-wrong. Within a GRPO group of N N rollouts for one question, we call the rollouts that emit a tool call the tool-using subgroup and the rest the no-tool subgroup , and the tool-using subgroup is all-wrong when none of its rollouts is correct, even if some no-tool rollouts in the same group succeed. Conditional on a question where tool use is attempted, how often does the tool-using subgroup fail together? 3(b) shows this all-wrong rate is ∼ \sim 40% for tool-using subgroups compared to ∼ \sim 25% for no-tool subgroups. Under group-normalized advantage, this asymmetry yields non-positive advantage on tool-call tokens in both regimes: in mixed groups they trail the no-tool success signal, and in fully all-wrong groups the numerator r i − mean ⁡ ( { r j } ) r_{i}-\operatorname{mean}(\{r_{j}\}) collapses to zero. Either way, effective learning signal on tool calls is suppressed on the questions where tool use would matter most. Tool calls admit substantive resampling at a fixed thinking. Resampling at the tool call is only worthwhile if it is a real divergence point under the policy. If the thinking prefix already commits to the concrete action, resampling at the tool-call boundary changes nothing. We probe this by decomposing a trajectory at the first tool-call boundary: we fix its thinking prefix 𝒕 1 {\bm{t}}_{1} , draw 16 continuations from π θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒙 , 𝒕 1 ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}},{\bm{t}}_{1}) , and cluster the resulting tool calls into semantic classes by an LLM judge that groups calls by their semantic intent. 3(c) shows that the resampled tool calls do not collapse to a single class. Across all tools, the 16 samples occupy 2.9–3.4 distinct semantic clusters on average. The thinking prefix therefore does not determine the exact tool call and the tool call is an under-explored divergence point whose exploration must be supplied externally. Takeaways: GRPO under-trains the tool call • Tool use remains a minority behavior under GRPO: ∼ \sim 20–35% of rollouts across RL steps, well below the thinking-only majority ( 3(a) ). • When attempted, the tool-using subgroup is all-wrong on ∼ \sim 40% of questions (vs. 25% for the no-tool subgroup), so tool-call tokens get negative advantage in mixed groups and zero in fully all-wrong groups ( 3(b) ). • Resampling from a fixed prefix preserves substantive diversity in the tool call (2.9–3.4 semantic clusters per 16 samples in 3(c) ): the tool call is a real divergence point. 3 Agent eXplorative Policy Optimization (AXPO) 3.1 Tool-call resampling In agentic reasoning, the policy must learn both thinking and tool use where the latter is the under-trained behavior under GRPO ( Section 2.2 ). Rather than scaling rollouts N N to generate tool-using successes uniformly, we commit to a thinking prefix that promises a tool call and concentrate stochasticity on the continuation. AXPO resamples only on groups in which the tool-using subgroup is non-empty and entirely wrong (an all-wrong tool-using subgroup ; no-tool rollouts in the same group may succeed). These are exactly the groups where tool-call tokens receive non-positive advantage under GRPO ( Section 2.2 ): zero when the entire group is all-wrong, negative when only no-tool rollouts succeed. A recovered continuation therefore delivers the largest gradient lift per resampled continuation. We use Qwen3-VL-Thinking [ 19 ] at three sizes (2B, 4B, 8B) as the base model across all methods. The tool set is the three families introduced in Section 2.1 : a Python interpreter, a web search engine (Tavily search API 1 1 1 https://www.tavily.com/ ), and an image zoom-in tool. All tools share a unified <tool_call> interface. Full prompt templates and tool schemas are in Appendix A.2 . Training data & pipeline. SFT uses 64K correct trajectories drawn from ViRL [ 35 ] , fvqa [ 36 ] , and PyVision-RL [ 18 ] , generated by Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking [ 19 ] where ∼ \sim 25% contain a tool call. RL uses a 16K filtered subset plus 22K questions from MMFineReason-hard [ 37 ] . We follow the SFT then RL pipeline of Section 2.1 . AXPO augments the rollout loop with tool-call resampling, holding all other hyperparameters constant against SFT + GRPO. Full details are in Appendix A.1 . Benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate on nine multimodal benchmarks grouped into three task categories: Reasoning (MathVision [ 38 ] , DynaMath [ 39 ] , Math-VR [ 40 ] ), Perception (V ⋆ [ 8 ] , VisualProbe [ 7 ] , HR-Bench-4K and HR-Bench-8K [ 41 ] ), and Search (HR-MMSearch [ 42 ] , MMSearch [ 43 ] ); per-benchmark descriptions in Appendix A.3 . All benchmarks are evaluated in the agentic setting with the same tool interface used in training. We report Pass@1 and Pass@4 (%), averaged over four rollouts per question, with answer matching logic tailored for each benchmark. Baselines. We compare AXPO against four baselines: (1) Base : the base model only with prompting without additional training (2) SFT : the SFT checkpoint without RL (3) GRPO : RL from the base model without an SFT stage and (4) SFT + GRPO : the standard SFT-then-RL recipe. Our method, SFT + AXPO : applies tool-call resampling and advantage calculation from Section 3 on top of the same SFT-then-RL pipeline. 4.2 Main Results: AXPO narrows the agentic gap to a 4 × \times larger baseline. Tools span knowledge search [ 5 , 4 ] , computation [ 10 , 11 , 49 , 50 , 51 ] , and visual perception [ 44 , 7 , 12 , 45 , 52 , 53 ] . Recent VLM systems combine image manipulation with code and search [ 43 , 23 , 18 , 14 , 54 ] , and follow a two-stage SFT-then-RL recipe. RL for agentic reasoning. On thinking-only trajectories, group-relative methods like GRPO [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] normalize rewards within N N rollouts and uniformly assign the resulting advantage; BroRL [ 30 ] analyzes how scaling N N closes coverage gaps. Three lines extend this family to tool-using rollouts: direct ports that reuse outcome-reward RL without changing the sampling structure [ 45 , 23 , 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 , 22 , 42 ] , mid-trajectory branching that resamples the continuation after a tool call to absorb tool-output uncertainty [ 31 , 59 ] , and reward shaping that adds bonus or penalty terms on tool use [ 18 , 29 ] . We include more detailed comparison with related works in Appendix C . Our contribution. AXPO contrasts with each line. Against direct use of GRPO, it restores learning signal on the all-wrong tool-using subgroups identified in Section 2.2 , which uniform sampling cannot reach. Against mid-trajectory branching [ 31 , 59 ] , it resamples at the tool-call boundary rather than after the tool observation, exploring the tool call itself rather than the continuation given a tool output. Against reward shaping, it acts on the rollout distribution while leaving the reward intact. 6 Conclusion We identified a Thinking-Acting Gap in group-based agentic RL, an asymmetry between thinking (the self-contained default) and tool use (a high-variance auxiliary) that manifests during training as two symptoms: tool use is attempted on a minority of rollouts and tool-using subgroups (the tool-using rollouts within a group) are disproportionately all-wrong, so the advantage at tool-call tokens is non-positive on exactly the questions where tool use would help. AXPO narrows this gap by augmenting the rollout loop with tool-call resampling , which fixes the thinking prefix and concentrates exploration on the tool call itself, paired with uncertainty-based prefix selection. Across nine multimodal benchmarks and three model scales, AXPO consistently outperforms SFT + GRPO, and at 8B it surpasses the 32B Base baseline on Pass@4 with 4 × 4\times fewer parameters. Limitations. Our study assumes verifiable outcome rewards for RL and trains models up to 8B parameters. We discuss limitations and the future directions in details in Appendix E . A.1 Training We expand on Section 4.1 with the full training data composition and hyperparameter list. SFT data composition. SFT uses 64,274 trajectories drawn from three sources: ViRL [ 35 ] , fvqa [ 36 ] , and PyVision-RL [ 18 ] . All trajectories are generated by Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking [ 19 ] acting as the teacher model. ∼ \sim 25% of the trajectories contain at least one tool call; the remainder solve the problem with internal reasoning alone. We retain only trajectories whose final answer is correct against the ground-truth label. RL data composition. RL uses 15,591 problems obtained by filtering the SFT problem set: we remove problems that the SFT checkpoint solves on all 4 rollouts, and problems that the 32B teacher fails on all 4 rollouts. This filtering convention follows prior agentic RL work [ 23 , 26 ] and removes both trivial problems (zero learning signal) and unreachable problems (no positive signal achievable at this scale). We additionally include 22,000 hard questions from MMFineReason-hard 2 2 2 A question subset of the MMFineReason corpus that Qwen3-VL-4B entirely fails on 4 rollouts. to expose the policy to problems unseen during SFT, bringing the RL training set to ∼ \sim 37K problems. A.2 System Prompt and Tool Interface We use the same agentic system prompt for SFT, RL, and evaluation across all model sizes where the prompt is modified version of the system prompt of deepeyes v2 [ 23 ] . Tools are exposed via a unified <tool_call> interface used in qwen-agent [ 19 ] and the model is free to invoke any subset of the three tools ( python , tavily-search , image_zoom_in ) on every question. The full text of the prompt is reproduced below. System Prompt You are an agent: please keep going until the user’s query is completely resolved, before ending your turn and yielding back to the user. Only terminate your turn when you are sure that the problem is solved. Solve the following problem step by step. In your reasoning process, if the answer cannot be determined, you can write Python code in a Jupyter Notebook to process the image and extract more information from it. The stdout and stderr content, along with the images generated by “ plt.show() ” will be returned to better assist with the user query. You MUST use the python tool to analyze or transform images whenever it could improve your understanding. This includes but is not limited to zooming in, rotating, adjusting contrast, computing statistics, or isolating features. If you find you lack sufficient knowledge to confidently answer the question, you MUST conduct search to thoroughly seek the internet for information. No matter how complex the query, you will not give up until you find the corresponding information. You can use the tavily-search tool, which will search the web and return relevant information based on your query. Notes for tools: ## image_zoom_in tool 1. image_zoom_in crops and magnifies a specific region of the image so you can inspect fine details. 2. When you need to look at a specific region more closely, prefer image_zoom_in over writing python code to crop — it is simpler, faster, and returns a high-resolution view directly. 3. After a zoom-in, the cropped image is appended to _pil_images in the python tool (the observation will tell you the exact index), so you can further process it with code if needed. ## python tool 1. python runs in a stateful Jupyter notebook kernel — variables, imports, and state persist across calls. 2. The conversation images are pre-loaded as _pil_images (list of PIL Image objects) and _images (list of file paths). Images produced by other tools (e.g. image_zoom_in ) are also appended to these lists. 3. Use plt.show() to visualize processed images; generated plots are automatically captured and returned. 4. Available packages include numpy, scipy, sympy, matplotlib, PIL/Pillow, and the standard library. 5. Always use Python for non-trivial computation — trigonometric calculations, multi-step arithmetic, equation solving, and area/volume formulas. Do NOT compute these mentally; write code to ensure numerical accuracy. 6. Your program should always return in finite time. Do not write infinite loops. 7. Writing file to disk is not allowed. ## tavily-search tool 1. You MUST engage in many interactions, delving deeply into the topic to explore all possible aspects until a satisfactory answer is found. 2. Before presenting a Final Answer, you will cross-check and validate the information you’ve gathered to confirm its accuracy and reliability. 3. You will carefully analyze each information source to ensure that all data is current, relevant, and from credible origins. ## general You MUST think and plan before each function call, and reflect on the outcomes of the previous function calls. DO NOT do this entire process by making function calls only, as this can impair your ability to solve the problem and think insightfully. Remember to place the final answer in the last part using the format: <answer> \boxed{"The final answer goes here."} </answer> Tool schemas. A.3 Benchmark Details We evaluate on nine multimodal benchmarks grouped by which tool family is most expected to help: Reasoning (Python interpreter), Perception (image zoom-in), and Search (web search). All benchmarks are evaluated in the agentic setting with the same tool interface used in training; the model is free to use any subset of the three tools or none at all on every question. Reasoning. These benchmarks evaluate multi-step reasoning over text, math, and figures, where a Python interpreter is the natural tool for symbolic and numerical computation. • MathVision [ 38 ] : competition-style math problems paired with diagrams (geometry, algebra, combinatorics). Answers are short numerical or symbolic expressions; we use the public mini test set containing 304 questions. • DynaMath [ 39 ] : a benchmark of programmatically generated math questions with multiple parametric variants per seed problem. We evaluate on a single-variant slice (501 seed problems). The benchmark complements MathVision as it provides additional algorithmically generated problems spanning plane geometry, statistics, and other domains with diverse difficulty. • Math-VR [ 40 ] : a mathematical visual reasoning benchmark introduced with CodePlot-CoT, in which problems are paired with diagrams (figures, plots, geometric constructions) that the model must inspect to compute the answer. The benchmark targets the regime where the visual content is load-bearing for the math derivation rather than decorative. Perception. These benchmarks contain high-resolution images with information that is hard to read at the default vision encoder resolution. The image zoom-in tool is the natural recovery mechanism. • V ⋆ [ 8 ] : a fine-grained visual-search benchmark in which the answer depends on a small object embedded in a complex scene. Designed to expose the failure of monolithic image encoders on high-resolution detail. • VisualProbe [ 7 ] : a multimodal probing benchmark introduced with mini-o3, where each question targets a specific small region (text, sign, label) within a high-resolution scene. We use the hard subset, which selects questions Qwen3-VL-Thinking-8B fails without tools. • HR-Bench-4K and HR-Bench-8K [ 41 ] : high-resolution single-image perception at 4096 2 4096^{2} and 8192 2 8192^{2} resolutions, respectively. Questions probe small text, distant objects, and fine textures; the two splits share a common question pool with images rescaled to the target resolution. Search. These benchmarks require external knowledge that is unlikely to be in the model’s parametric memory or that requires multi-hop lookup. The Tavily web search API is the natural tool. • HR-MMSearch [ 42 ] : high-resolution multimodal search questions whose answers are composed by chaining two or more web lookups (e.g., “in which year was the mayor of the city where this fashion designer was born”). The benchmark stresses both perception (identifying entities from the image) and multi-hop search composition. • MMSearch [ 43 ] : an earlier multimodal search benchmark covering current-events questions whose answers depend on web content released after the model’s training cutoff. Predominantly single-hop, but answers are often time-sensitive. Evaluation protocol. For all benchmarks, we draw four rollouts per question and report Pass@1 (per-question accuracy averaged over four rollouts) and Pass@4 (a question is correct if any of the four rollouts is correct). Final-answer matching against the gold label is performed by an exact match for math and multiple-choice question and F1 score for search questions. For benchmarks that are hard to evaluate with exact match (e.g., MMSearch), we use a llm-as-a-judge using gpt-5-mini model. Comparing Non-agent and Base at the same model size measures the effect of turning tools on without any training . The gain is strongly scale-dependent: Pass@1 / Pass@4 deltas are − 1.3 -1.3 / + 1.1 +1.1 at 2B, + 5.2 +5.2 / + 9.2 +9.2 at 4B, + 4.7 +4.7 / + 9.8 +9.8 at 8B, and + 6.7 +6.7 / + 10.1 +10.1 at 32B. At 2B the Base (agentic) baseline is actually worse than the Non-agent baseline on Pass@1, showing that small models pay an agent-prompt overhead that outweighs the gain from correct tool use. Larger models recover Pass@1 and accumulate a Pass@4 ceiling gain, but even at 32B the gap to SFT + AXPO at 8B on Pass@4 ( 75.8 75.8 vs. 75.1 75.1 ) shows that inference-time tool access alone does not close the agentic gap. Post-training is therefore necessary at every trainable scale. Why SFT before RL? Comparing GRPO (RL from base) against SFT + GRPO measures the value of an SFT initialization before RL. Pass@1 gaps shrink with size ( + 5.3 +5.3 at 2B, + 5.2 +5.2 at 4B, + 1.3 +1.3 at 8B), but Pass@4 gaps remain positive at every scale ( + 6.8 +6.8 , + 4.9 +4.9 , + 2.4 +2.4 ). RL from the base policy can find a single high-reward mode (Pass@1 partially recovered at 8B), but it consistently sacrifices diversity, capping the Pass@4 ceiling [ 62 ] . SFT broadens the cold-start distribution over tool-using trajectories before group-based exploration begins. Without it, all-wrong tool-using subgroups dominate from step 1 and the policy collapses onto a narrow single-mode solution [ 23 ] . Why RL after SFT? SFT minimizes log-likelihood on a fixed set of teacher trajectories: it can make the student imitate the teacher’s tool-use patterns, but the optimization signal lives entirely on the teacher’s distribution. At test time the student samples from its own distribution and small token-level deviations from the teacher accumulate into prefixes the SFT objective never scored, so imitation alone does not guarantee that on-policy rollouts inherit the teacher’s correctness ( exposure bias ). RL after SFT narrows this gap by training on the policy’s own rollouts under an outcome reward, adapting the policy to its own induced trajectory distribution rather than to the teacher’s [ 63 ] . Empirically, comparing SFT against SFT + GRPO isolates this on-policy adaptation effect given the SFT initialization: Pass@1 improves at every scale ( + 4.5 +4.5 at 2B, + 1.2 +1.2 at 4B, + 2.0 +2.0 at 8B), the regime where on-policy reliability matters most, while Pass@4 gains are smaller and uneven ( + 2.3 +2.3 , + 0.0 +0.0 , + 1.8 +1.8 ), consistent with GRPO consolidating mass on trajectories the SFT policy can already reach rather than discovering new ones. RL is therefore necessary on top of SFT, but standard GRPO’s adaptation is biased toward the SFT manifold, motivating AXPO’s tool-call resampling. Why AXPO on top of SFT, instead of GRPO? The previous two paragraphs leave a structural gap: SFT sets the Pass@4 ceiling and RL sharpens within it, so further gains require a mechanism that simultaneously extends the ceiling and sharpens. AXPO does both. Pass@1 gains over SFT + GRPO are + 1.1 +1.1 / + 1.4 +1.4 / + 1.8 +1.8 at 2B/4B/8B, and Pass@4 gains are + 2.8 +2.8 / + 2.3 +2.3 / + 1.8 +1.8 . The Pass@4 lift is the diagnostic signature that AXPO operates on a different axis from SFT-then-GRPO sharpening: by recovering all-wrong tool-using subgroups whose gradient signal would otherwise vanish ( Section 2.2 ), AXPO turns previously dead continuations into trainable ones, expanding the policy’s reachable correct-trajectory set rather than only redistributing mass within it. B.9 Confidence as a Tractable Proxy for Tool-Call Entropy Section 3 ranks candidate prefixes by the mean probability the source policy assigned to the tool-call tokens of τ src \tau^{\text{src}} (henceforth confidence ). The natural alternative is the predictive entropy H ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒙 , 𝒚 < t ) ) H(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t})) of the next-token distribution at each tool-call position, but this choice is precluded by training-loop structure. Per-token sampling probabilities are emitted essentially for free by the rollout engine (vLLM [ 65 ] ), whereas predictive entropy requires either an extra forward pass over the full vocabulary under the trained policy (FSDP) or vLLM-side full-vocabulary logprob expansion at decode time. Our RL pipeline under verl [ 60 ] alternates rollout (vLLM) and gradient updates (FSDP), so inserting a per-prefix entropy computation would force an additional vLLM → \to FSDP → \to vLLM round-trip per training step (or equivalently expensive vLLM-side full-vocabulary logprob expansion), a cost we wished to avoid. To verify that confidence preserves the ranking an entropy-based scheme would induce, we measured the per-step correlation between mean-token-confidence and exact policy entropy on tool-call positions of failed tool-using rollouts collected during training ( Figure 6 ). Across training steps, the two signals are strongly correlated (Pearson ρ = 0.843 \rho=0.843 , Spearman ρ = 0.835 \rho=0.835 , OLS fit y = 0.41 ​ x + 0.07 y=0.41x+0.07 on entropy vs negated confidence). Confidence therefore preserves the relative ordering an entropy-based scheme would produce, and we adopt it as the ranking signal in AXPO. Appendix C Extended Related Works This appendix expands on Section 5 with the longer descriptions that the main text abridges. Two-stage SFT-then-RL recipe for agentic VLMs. Recent agentic VLM systems share a two-stage recipe: supervised fine-tuning on tool-using trajectories distilled from larger teachers [ 66 , 20 ] , followed by outcome-reward RL [ 18 , 23 , 45 ] . They differ mainly in the distillation corpus, the tool interface, and the choice of base model. Most prior agentic-RL VLM studies focus on a single tool family (typically image manipulation), whereas our setup combines code, search, and image zoom-in on a thinking-capable base (Qwen3-VL-Thinking) [ 19 ] , a configuration under which the RL stage becomes the primary bottleneck. Group-relative RL and BroRL. RL with verifiable outcome rewards is the standard post-SFT stage for reasoning models [ 1 , 2 ] . GRPO [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] samples N N rollouts per question, normalizes rewards within the group, and assigns the resulting advantage uniformly to every token. BroRL [ 30 ] argues that increasing N N reduces unsampled blind spots at a rate determined by per-token baseline probability. Both analyses were developed for thinking-only trajectories, where the rollout structure is uniform across tokens and the per-token baseline probability decays slowly. Proposition 1 shows that AXPO’s prefix-fixed resampling dominates raw scaling in the regime where tool-call tokens sit at low policy probability, exactly the failure mode Section 2.2 diagnoses. Mid-trajectory branching for tool-using RL. ARPO [ 31 ] and AEPO [ 59 ] adapt group-relative RL to tool-using rollouts by branching after a tool observation, drawing additional continuations from π θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒙 , 𝒕 1 , 𝒂 1 , 𝒐 1 ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}},{\bm{t}}_{1},{\bm{a}}_{1},{\bm{o}}_{1}) when post-observation entropy is high. The exploration target is the continuation given a fixed tool call, which absorbs variance introduced by the tool output but cannot recover when the tool call itself is wrong (wrong sub-image, wrong python code, wrong search query). AXPO instead branches at the tool-call boundary and triggers only on all-wrong tool-using subgroups, with a per-prefix advantage that credits the source prefix exactly when its branched continuation succeeds, making it a targeted intervention on the regime Section 2.2 identifies as binding rather than a general rollout-budget reshaper. Empirically, AXPO outperforms ARPO on the 8B comparison ( 53.9 53.9 vs. 51.3 51.3 Avg, Table 3 ), consistent with the diagnosis that the tool call itself, not the post-observation continuation, is the dominant failure locus. The two strategies are compatible, and combining tool-call and post-observation branching is a natural extension we leave to future work. Appendix E Limitations and Future Work We expand on the limitations sketched in the main-text conclusion and discuss future directions. Verifiable outcome rewards. AXPO’s subgroup-level trigger (“all-wrong tool-using subgroup”) and per-prefix advantage in Eq. 2 both rely on a binary, automatically verifiable outcome signal r ∈ { 0 , 1 } r\in\{0,1\} . Tasks where verifiability is partial (open-ended generation [ 67 , 68 ] , multi-criterion subjective evaluation) require a different definition of “failed subgroup” before tool-call resampling applies. The resampling mechanism itself is reward-agnostic, but the trigger and the all-wrong learning signal argument in Section 2.2 are not. Compute scope of training. Trained models are at most 8B parameters; 32B is reported inference-only as the SFT teacher. This boundary reflects available compute rather than a methodological choice [ 69 , 68 , 70 , 71 , 72 ] . Whether the Thinking-Acting Gap and AXPO’s recovery generalize to 32B+ trainable scale, where the base policy is closer to the tool-use ceiling and the all-wrong-subgroup fraction may be smaller, is open. Furthermore, although the teacher model can theoretically scale to 100B+ parameters, analyzing the effects of teacher scaling on downstream reinforcement learning (RL) remains an area for future work. Future work: richer tool environments. Our tool inventory covers three families that span numerical, retrieval, and visual modalities (Python interpreter, web search, image zoom-in), each shown to be load-bearing in prior agentic VLM work [ 23 , 18 , 7 ] ; this multi-tool setup is already broader than most prior agentic-VLM RL studies, which typically focus on a single tool family. One notable absence is an image-search tool, which prior works [ 23 , 42 ] report results with but which we could not include during training and full evaluation due to per-call API costs at our scale (we instead approximate it via a GPT-5.4 prompt for the unseen-tool study in Appendix B.5 ). Tools with longer execution latency (browser agents, GUI control, terminal sessions) and tools with high per-call cost (LLM-as-tool) [ 13 ] introduce additional considerations that we do not address. Extending AXPO to such richer [ 73 , 74 , 75 ] , longer-horizon environments is a natural next step. Future work: generalization to other base models. All experiments use Qwen3-VL-Thinking, which is currently the strongest open thinking-capable VLM with reliable tool-using ability and the model best supported by our RL framework. The Thinking-Acting Gap is a property of RL on an agentic reasoning model rather than of any specific architecture [ 76 , 77 , 78 , 79 ] , and we expect the diagnostics and AXPO’s coverage gain to transfer; replicating on the most recent Qwen3.5 models [ 80 ] , once RL framework support matures, would help establish the gap as a general phenomenon and rule out base-specific confounds. Appendix F Broader Impacts AXPO is a methodological improvement to the RL training of agentic VLMs and is additive on top of a publicly released base model (Qwen3-VL-Thinking [ 19 ] ), so it does not introduce a new capability class. Among the three tool families used in this work, the Python interpreter raises standard security concerns for code-executing agents. We can run all tool calls in a sandboxed execution environment during both training and evaluation, consistent with prior agentic-VLM RL work [ 12 ] . Beyond this sandboxing, broader safety considerations [ 81 , 82 , 83 , 84 , 85 , 86 , 87 ] (e.g., misuse of tool-grounded outputs, causality, robustness, deployment-time guardrails, downstream effects of cheaper agentic deployments) are out of scope for this work and were not addressed.
